title: Human rights, race equality and reasonable adjustments
blurb: Apply HRA Articles 2, 3, 5 and 8 in detention, tackle racial inequality under the MHA and make reasonable adjustments.
question: Devon, a young Black man detained under section 3, says staff treat him as 'dangerous' and that he is not allowed to phone his family. A colleague says this is just ward policy. Which rights and duties should guide the nurse's response?

teach.h: Rights do not stop at the ward door
teach.body: NHS bodies are public authorities and must act compatibly with the European Convention rights in the Human Rights Act 1998 (HRA). They must also meet the Equality Act 2010, including reasonable adjustments and the public sector equality duty. The Code of Practice says lawful MHA decisions include compliance with both Acts (COP15 1.22). In plain English: detention limits some freedoms, but every limit must be lawful, necessary, proportionate and fair.

teach.h: Articles most used in mental health care
head: Article
Right
In practice
rows: Reasonable steps to protect detained patients at risk
No torture, inhuman or degrading treatment
Lawful detention of 'unsound mind'; speedy court review (5(4))
Qualified: limits must be lawful, necessary, proportionate
teach.caption: Article 5(4) is why detained patients can apply to the tribunal. Blanket bans engage Article 8.
NHS England Digital, MHA Statistics 2024-25: Black people nearly 4 times more likely to be detained, over 8.5 times more likely to be on a CTO.

teach.body: The Patient and Carer Race Equality Framework (PCREF), published by NHS England in October 2023, is mandatory for NHS mental health trusts through the NHS Standard Contract. It has three parts: legislative and regulatory obligations (leadership and governance); six national organisational competencies, including cultural awareness, co-production and workforce; and a patient and carer feedback mechanism. Each trust needs a board-level lead and a local plan, co-produced with communities and published annually.

teach.h: Is this a disability? (Equality Act s6)

steps.label: Long-term?
steps.sub: 12 months+, likely to, or likely to recur

teach.caption: Sch 1 para 2: an effect that is likely to recur is treated as continuing.

teach.h: Reasonable adjustments in mental health care
items: Adjust practices: longer appointments, a quiet waiting area, flexible times for someone with anxiety.
Provide information in an accessible format such as easy read (s20(6)), and auxiliary aids such as a BSL interpreter where needed (s20(5)).
Never charge the person for the adjustment (s20(7)).
Challenge stigma and diagnostic overshadowing: do not put physical symptoms down to mental illness without assessment.

teach.body: A blanket phone ban interferes with Devon's Article 8 right; any restriction must be individually assessed, lawful, necessary and proportionate, and recorded. Labelling him 'dangerous' without evidence risks discrimination (Article 14, Equality Act race and disability protection) and racial stereotyping that PCREF exists to tackle. The nurse listens, reviews his individual risk plan, restores contact unless a specific justified reason exists, offers an IMHA and raises the concern with the ward manager.

teach.text: Article 8 is QUALIFIED: it can be limited if lawful, necessary and proportionate. Article 3 is ABSOLUTE: inhuman or degrading treatment can never be justified, whatever the risk or staffing pressure. Do not mix them up.

items: HRA: Article 2 life, 3 no inhuman or degrading treatment (absolute), 5 liberty with speedy review, 8 private and family life (qualified), 14 non-discrimination.
Black people were nearly 4 times as likely to be detained and over 8.5 times as likely to be on a CTO (2024-25).
PCREF: mandatory anti-racism framework for mental health trusts, three parts, co-produced annual plan.
Equality Act: mental impairment can be a disability; reasonable adjustments, free of charge; challenge stigma.

summary: You can now apply the key HRA articles to detention and ward restrictions, describe racial inequality in use of the MHA and PCREF's response, and make reasonable adjustments for people with mental health conditions. You can tell absolute from qualified rights.

A.q: Which Human Rights Act article gives a detained patient the right to have the lawfulness of detention decided speedily by a court?
A.why: Article 5(4): everyone deprived of liberty is entitled to proceedings by which the lawfulness of detention is decided speedily by a court. The tribunal provides this.

whyNot.1: Article 8 protects private and family life.
whyNot.2: Article 3 prohibits torture and inhuman or degrading treatment.
whyNot.3: Article 14 prohibits discrimination in the enjoyment of Convention rights.

A.q: Which right in the Human Rights Act is absolute and cannot be limited for any reason?
options: Right to respect for private and family life
Freedom of thought, conscience and religion
Right to liberty and security of person
Prohibition of inhuman or degrading treatment
A.why: Article 3 contains no exceptions: no one shall be subjected to torture or inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment.

whyNot.0: Article 8 is qualified and can be limited where lawful, necessary and proportionate.
whyNot.1: Article 9 allows limits on manifesting religion or belief.
whyNot.2: Article 5 permits lawful detention in listed cases, including of persons of unsound mind.

A.q: Under the Equality Act 2010, when is a mental health condition's effect treated as long-term?
options: It has lasted or is likely to last 12 months
It has lasted at least 6 months
It has led to a hospital admission under the MHA
It has lasted at least 3 months
A.why: Schedule 1 para 2: long-term means it has lasted, or is likely to last, at least 12 months, or for the rest of the person's life; a recurring effect counts.

whyNot.1: Six months is not the statutory test.
whyNot.2: Admission is not part of the definition.
whyNot.3: Three months is not the statutory test.

B.q: A ward bans all patients from using mobile phones, without individual assessment. Which right is most directly engaged?
B.why: Contact with family and correspondence fall within Article 8; a blanket restriction must be justified as lawful, necessary and proportionate.

whyNot.0: Article 2 concerns protection of life, not communication.
whyNot.2: A phone ban is unlikely to reach the severity of Article 3, though it may be unlawful under Article 8.
whyNot.3: Article 5 concerns deprivation of liberty, not phone access.

B.q: According to NHS England Digital's 2024-25 Mental Health Act statistics, how did detention rates for Black or Black British people compare with White people?
options: About ten times the White rate
B.why: In 2024-25 the detention rate for Black or Black British people was 262.4 per 100,000, nearly four times the White rate of 65.8.

whyNot.0: There is a large disparity, not parity.
whyNot.1: The gap is wider than double.
whyNot.2: Ten times overstates the broad-group disparity in detentions.

B.q: What is the Patient and Carer Race Equality Framework (PCREF)?
options: A tribunal procedure rule on using interpreters
A voluntary e-learning module for ward staff
A mandatory anti-racism framework for trusts
A section of the Mental Health Act 1983
B.why: PCREF, published by NHS England in October 2023, is a mandatory framework (via the NHS Standard Contract) for mental health trusts and providers to tackle racial inequality.

whyNot.0: PCREF is an organisational framework, not a tribunal rule.
whyNot.1: It is mandatory and organisation-wide, not a voluntary training module.
whyNot.3: It is NHS England guidance, not part of the Act.

C.q: Aaron, who has severe social anxiety, misses repeated clinic appointments because he cannot face the busy waiting room. The clinic proposes discharge for non-attendance. What is the most appropriate response?
options: Discharge him under the clinic's policy
Offer a quieter or remote appointment
Charge him for the missed slots
Refer him to the GP to rebook
C.why: His anxiety may be a disability under s6; the s20 duty requires reasonable adjustments to practices, such as a quiet space or remote appointment, at no cost to him.

whyNot.0: Applying the policy rigidly may fail the reasonable adjustments duty.
whyNot.2: Adjustments must not be charged for (s20(7)), and charging would deter attendance.
whyNot.3: Passing him back without adjustment leaves the barrier in place.

C.q: Devon, detained under section 3, is told he cannot phone his family because 'all patients on this ward lose phones for the first week'. What should the nurse do first?
options: Explain the ward rule to him and record his complaint
Ask his family to visit in place of calls
Review whether a restriction is justified for him
Wait for the tribunal to decide
C.why: A blanket rule interferes with Article 8 without individual justification; restrictions must be assessed for the individual as lawful, necessary and proportionate.

whyNot.0: Recording the complaint is right, but enforcing an unjustified blanket rule is not.
whyNot.1: Visits do not justify an unassessed ban on calls.
whyNot.3: Tribunals review detention, not ward phone rules; the nurse can act now.

C.q: Mr Ali, who has schizophrenia, reports new chest pain. A colleague says 'it's probably his anxiety, he's always worried'. What does this illustrate and what should happen?
options: Appropriate caution: wait and review at handover
C.why: Attributing a physical symptom to mental illness without assessment is diagnostic overshadowing, a form of stigma; the pain needs prompt physical assessment.

whyNot.1: Delaying assessment of chest pain is unsafe.
whyNot.2: Positive risk-taking does not mean ignoring new physical symptoms.
whyNot.3: Least restriction is about liberty, not withholding assessment.

reteach.title: Lawful, necessary, proportionate, fair
reteach.question: What four tests should every restriction on a mental health ward pass?

blocks.body: LAWFUL: is there a legal power (the MHA, MCA, a policy based on law)? NECESSARY: is it needed for this person now? PROPORTIONATE: is it the least restrictive way to meet the need? FAIR: is it applied without discrimination, with reasonable adjustments? Article 3 is different: degrading treatment is never justified, whatever the reason.

blocks.text: Blanket restrictions applied to everyone on a ward are hard to justify under Article 8, because they are not based on individual assessment.

explain.body: Article 5(1)(e) permits lawful detention of persons of unsound mind under a procedure prescribed by law; Article 5(4) gives speedy court review. Article 2 requires reasonable protective steps; Article 3 is absolute; Article 8 is qualified.

test.q: Which article permits the lawful detention of 'persons of unsound mind'?
test.why: Article 5(1)(e) lists the lawful detention of persons of unsound mind as a permitted deprivation of liberty.

whyNot.1: Article 3 prohibits inhuman or degrading treatment.
whyNot.2: Article 8 protects private and family life.

explain.body: Black or Black British people were detained at nearly four times the rate of White people in 2024-25 and were over 8.5 times as likely to be on a CTO. PCREF requires trusts to act, with communities.

test.q: How many core parts does PCREF have?
test.why: PCREF has three parts: legislative and regulatory obligations, national organisational competencies, and a patient and carer feedback mechanism.

whyNot.0: There are three parts, not two.
whyNot.2: There are three parts, not four.
whyNot.3: Six is the number of national organisational competencies within Part 2.

explain.body: A mental impairment with a substantial, long-term adverse effect on day-to-day activities is a disability (s6). Service providers must make reasonable adjustments, free of charge (s20).

test.q: Who pays for a reasonable adjustment made for a disabled patient?
test.why: Equality Act s20(7): the disabled person must not be charged for the cost of complying with the duty.

whyNot.0: Charging the disabled person is prohibited.
whyNot.1: The family is not liable for the provider's duty.
whyNot.3: The duty falls on the provider making the adjustment.

explain.body: Stigma shows as stereotyping (for example 'dangerous'), exclusion and diagnostic overshadowing. Use person-first language, base risk on evidence, and assess new physical symptoms properly.

test.q: Which phrase best reflects person-first, non-stigmatising language?
test.why: Person-first language names the person before the condition and avoids labels.

whyNot.0: This defines him by his diagnosis.
whyNot.1: This reduces him to a symptom.
